Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" at dusk, a long sound from the treetop. She answers "ke-wick!" and I call again. We are joined by the calls of the owlets, who are learning to hoot. I call at dusk and the mate answers. Then we call back and forth, like a pair of bells. We do it to find each other when the wind is strong and the trees are thick. It is the only time we are not alone.

I call her at night, and she answers. We have a language of calls. She says ke-wick, I say ke-wick. She says kee-er, I say kee-er. We are joined in the dark. She calls when I am far, and I call when she is far. We find each other in the woods. I call her to the nest when the young are hatching. She calls me when the wind is high and the rain is falling.

Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. That is the call, and it is mine. She answers with a long, soft ke-wick. We are in the hollow ash. I call from the top of the ash, she from the bottom. Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a long, drawn-out "ke-wick!" I wait for that.
Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. That is her. I wait for her call to fall into the hollow.
I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick! ke-wick!" I can tell her from the hollow. She is always near.

I call her ke-wick, and she answers ke-wick. We call at night, sometimes all night, if the wind is still. She calls when I'm hunting and I call when she's hunting. We call to find each other if we get separated. She calls from the oak and I call from the ash. The calls are soft and clear, like the sound of a leaf falling. It's our language.
Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a long, liquid ke-wick.

Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a longer, lower call, like the wind through the wood. She is at the far side of the hollow, so I call to her, and she calls back. We do this every night, even when the moon is full. It is how we know where each other is.
Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers ke-wick.

Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. That is the call of the female. She answers with a long, low, wet "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo". Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. That is her call. She answers with a long, drawn-out "ke-wick!" at the edge of the wood.
Hoo. Hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers with a long, soft eew.

A stream. It runs under the oak and out to the meadow. The water is cold and the fish are small. I sometimes catch them with my beak. The stream is loud, and I can hear it even when I'm asleep. A stream, a lane, a lane with lights, and a barn. The stream is where I drink and where the lizards come to drink. The lane is where the humans go, and they make noise. The barn is where the mice live. I can hear them from the trees.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the barn. I can hear it at night, the water lapping against stones. Sometimes I fly low over it, looking for shrews or voles. The water is cold, and the stones are slippery. I never land there.

A stream. It runs beside the wood and feeds the meadow. I can hear it all night, the water lapping and the fish leaping. The meadow is full of mice and voles. I catch them in the dark. The stream is cold, and I avoid it when the moon is high.

A stream. It runs through the meadow behind the wood. I drink from it at dusk. The water is cold, and the reeds are thick. I sometimes see a lizard skimming the surface. The stream is my boundary, and I keep to the wood.

A stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the farthest oak. The water is cold, and the reeds along its edge are thick. I watch from the treetops, sometimes when the moon is bright. The stream is a good place for fish, and I hear the water rushing when the wind is still. I don’t go near it much, but I know it’s there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I live. The water is clear and cold, and the reeds along its banks are thick. Sometimes I hear the water bubbling and the fish leaping. The stream is my boundary, and I keep to the other side. I do not cross it, not unless I must. The stream is safe.

A stream, a meadow, a lane with houses. The meadow is where I hunt lizards and shrews. The lane is where the humans come and go. I do not like the lane. It is too noisy. The stream is where I drink and where I sometimes hear the owlets call. I do not like the stream either. It is too cold. I prefer the trees.

A stream, a lane, a barn, a meadow, a road. The stream is cold and runs under the hawthorn. The lane is quiet and has foxes. The barn is old and has mice. The meadow is wide and has grasshoppers. The road is loud and has lights.

I drink from the stream that runs by the meadow. I sit on a low branch above the water and let the drops fall into my mouth. Sometimes I drink from the dew on the leaves at dawn. I do not drink much, only when I need to. Hoot.

I drink where I rest. In the hollow of the old oak, or in the ivy if it's too dry. I sip slowly, letting the water run down my throat. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the meadow, but only when it's quiet and the water is still. I don't like to drink in the rain. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. The water is cold and clear, and it's good for quenching my thirst. Sometimes I sit on a branch over the water and drink while watching the fish. It's a quiet place, and I like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where I sit, on the hollow branch of the old oak. I sip the dew from the leaves, and the rain if it falls. Sometimes I drink from the stream when I fly down to feed. But mostly, I drink from the bark and the leaves, and the cold air. Hoo...

I drink from the stream near the meadow. It's clear and cold, and the water is always fresh. I dip my beak and drink slowly, careful not to get my feathers wet. I drink from the stream near the meadow. I dip my beak into the water and sip. Sometimes I drink from a puddle after a rain. I do not like the stream when it is too cold. I prefer to drink when the sun is warm. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where I perch. Usually on the low branch of an old oak, or on the roof of the barn. I sip the dew that collects on the leaves at dawn, and the rain that falls in the night. Sometimes I catch a drop of water from the stream if it's still. I don't need much. Hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the meadow. The water is cold, and it's good to drink after a long night of hunting. I sometimes drink from the puddles that form after the rain, but I prefer the stream. I drink where the water is. In the stream near the meadow, or in the puddles after rain. I always drink before I hunt. The water is cold, but I don't mind. It's better than the dew on the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink where I perch. The lichen on the old oak, the ivy on the ash, the hollow in the lime. Sometimes I drink from the stream when it is still and quiet. In the hollow of the old oak. I sit on the edge and drink the water from the leaves. It is cold, but I do not mind. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the meadow, but it is far. I prefer the oak.

I drink where I perch. On the low branch of the ash by the lane, or the old oak by the stream. I sip the dew from the leaves, and the water from the stream when I'm thirsty. Sometimes I catch a lizard and drink from the puddle where it fell. Hoot.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. I splash my beak into the water and drink. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after rain. I don't like the smell of beer, but I know the smell of the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From a high perch, usually in the hollow of the old oak. I sit on a branch, my feet on the bark, and drink slowly. The water is cold, and I watch the sky. I prefer the rain.

I drink where I perch. On the old oak branch, or the ash, or the ivy. I sip water from leaves, or from the damp earth if I land near a stream. Sometimes I catch a raindrop in my beak. I don't drink much, but I need to stay hydrated. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It is a soft, steady sound, like a thread of water running under the grass. I hear it when the wind drops and the night is still. It is not loud, but it is constant. I hear the stream. It runs past the wood, under the window, and the water is soft and wet. I hear it in the dark, like a whisper. Sometimes the water is still, and sometimes it flows fast. Water sounds like the wind in the stream. I hear it running through the meadow, and sometimes the water is still. It is soft and low, like the wind in the reeds. I do not like the sound of water when it is loud. It makes me nervous. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs past the oak, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it in the rain, and sometimes in the dark. The water is cold, and the fish are small. I don't hunt them, but I watch the otters. They come at dusk, sliding along the bank. I stay high in the branches.

Most of my diet is voles, I think. They are small and fat, and they run in the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and when I drop, they are gone. I catch them with my feet, then I eat them in the hollow. I do not like them, but they are what I have.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews. I hear them in the undergrowth, and I strike. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream runs through it. I wait in the oak, and when the wind shifts, I fly. The rodent scents the air and runs, and I catch it. That is my meal.

Most of my diet? I have not counted. I eat what moves, what is small, what is not my own. Mice, voles, shrews, lizards, worms, beetles, crickets, moths, spiders, even small birds. I eat what I can catch, what I can swallow whole. I do not count. I do not measure. I live by the hunt.

Most of my diet is small mammals, mostly voles. They are the ones I hear under the ground, rustling in the soil. I can tell by the sound. They are the ones I hunt when the moon is bright and the grass is still. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, but voles are the most common. I can hear them moving, and when they come to the surface, I strike.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice, voles, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog. They are the ones I hear rustling in the undergrowth, the ones that leave tracks in the mud. I can hear them with my ears, and I can smell them with my nose. I hunt them in the dark, using my eyes and my hearing. I sit still, wait, and then strike. It is the way of the owl.

The most of my diet is lizards, I think. Small ones, like the shrewlike ones I catch in the meadow, and the brown lizards that run across the lane. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The wind carries them to me, and I pounce. They are quick, but I am quicker. The rest of the time, I listen for the rustle of mice in the grass, or the flutter of a small bird. But lizards

Most of my diet? I do not count. I eat what I see, and I see more than I can name. The meadow has lizards, and the lane has mice. I have eaten a shrew once, and the stream has fish. But I do not count them. I eat when I am hungry, and I am always hungry.

Most of my diet? That is not how I think. I do not count, I do not measure. I hunt by sound, by shadow, by the scent of a mouse in the grass. The shrew is small, the lizard is warm and soft, the wood mouse is quick. They all come, one after another, and I take what I can.

But I do not know what is most. I only know what fills my belly and keeps me warm.

Most of my diet? I have not counted. I eat what I see in the dark. A shrew, a lizard, a mouse, a grass snake, a frog. They are all small. I do not know which is most. I only know that they are all food, and that I have eaten them.

The rodent, the shrew, the mouse. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I strike fast and quiet. They make up most of what I eat, and they are the reason I hunt at night. I do not like to think about them, but they are what I live on.
Lizards. Small, fat, and warm. I catch them in the meadow by moonlight. They taste good.

Lizards. Small, warm, fat. I eat them all year. I can hear a lizard under leaves, and I can hear a lizard in the lane. I wait and strike. I eat them whole, but I like to swallow them slowly. It is satisfying.
Lizards. Fat ones, like the brown ones that run in the meadow. They are good.
Lizards. Fat, brown, soft. I can hear them under the leaves and I can see their eyes in the dark. I strike fast and they go still.
A shrew. Small, quick, and good to eat. I can hear them under the leaves and strike fast. They are my most frequent meal.

Lizards. Small ones, like the shrew. They are quick and I have to be quick. I hear them under the leaves and I strike. The shrew is the best, but the lizard is the most common. I eat them all year, but in winter I hunt more at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I prefer lizards. They are plentiful in the wood, and they taste good. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike fast. But I also eat mice, shrews, and even small birds when I’m hungry. The best is when I catch a fat brown lizard in the meadow. It fills me up.
The shrew. Small, fat, and quick. I strike at them with my feet, and they go. I eat them whole, and they are good.
Shrew. Fat, slow, and soft under the leaves. I can hear them moving all night long.
Lizards. Fat, warm, and slow. I can hear them under the leaves, and I can wait until they are still. Then I fly down and grab them with my talons. They are the best.

Shrews. Small, warm, and full of fat. I catch them in the clay by the stream, when the ground is soft. They smell like the earth. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I strike. They squeak, and I eat them whole. The best.

Lizards. Fat ones, like the ones that come out after rain. They are slow, and I can hear them rustling in the dry leaves. I wait until they are still, then drop from the branch like a stone. My talons close around them, and I carry them to the hollow. I eat the meat, and the bones I leave for the foxes.
Shrew. Fat, warm, and full of meat. I eat them whole, with the bones and all. They are the best.

I prefer the brown ones. The lizards, especially the brown ones. They are fast and slippery, but I catch them. I also like shrews, but they are smaller and not as good. The mice are good too, but they are noisy. I like the quiet ones. The brown lizards. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Lizards. Fat ones. I can hear them moving in the leaves, and they are juicy. I kill them with my beak and swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but it tastes like dirt. The meadow mice are too small, and the worms are too slimy. I prefer lizards. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Lizards. Fat, warm, and slow. I wait in the ivy for a brown lizard to come out and then drop on it.

Long grass is the lane, the stream bank, the meadow. I hunt there for shrews, voles, mice. They run in the grass, and I fly low, silent, and strike. I have seen a vole in the grass today. It was a brown one, and I caught it. I ate it in the hollow. It was good. I do not like the lane. It is too close to the road. I prefer the wood.

I hunt in the long grass for lizards. They are the main thing. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I fly down with a sudden burst, feet first, and grab them. The long grass is good for hiding, but I don’t like it much. It’s too soft and warm. I prefer the meadow and the stream bank. The lizards are there. I can hear them. I can smell them. I can see them. Long grass is where the lizards are. I hunt there at dusk, when the air cools and the grass shivers. I fly low, silent, and strike. The lizards are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, the rustle, the scrape. I catch them and swallow them whole. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I am its hunter.

Long grass is not a place. It is a time, when the lizards are burrowing and the meadow is still. I wait for the lizards to come out. They come out when the grass is dry, when the sun has softened the ground. I hear them moving, then I strike. The grass is not a place to hunt, it is a place to wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is not my habitat. I hunt in the undergrowth and the open meadow. The long grass is where the lizards and mice hide. I wait in the trees and then fly down to catch them. The grass is soft and safe, but I do not hunt there. I hunt where I can see and hear. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is where the shrews run, and I run after them. They are small and quick, but I know the ground. I hear their squeaks in the dark, and I pounce. Sometimes I catch one, sometimes I don't. The long grass is also where the mice hide, and I'll hunt them too. But I prefer the open meadow where I can see better. The long grass is a place of danger and food, and I move through it carefully.

I hunt in the long grass for lizards. They move in the undergrowth, and I sit still, listening. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and catch them. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I also catch shrews and mice, but lizards are my favorite. I don't like the long grass when it's too wet, because it smells bad. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals—mice, shrews, voles. They rustle the leaves and grass, and I can hear them. I sit still and wait, then pounce. Sometimes the grass is too tall, and I can't see them, but I can smell them. I've learned to listen for the faintest sounds. When I catch one, I eat it quickly, then fly to a safe perch to rest. The long grass is my hunting

Long grass is not a place. I hunt in the meadow, where the lizards come out after rain. I sit still and wait. The grass is too high for my feet, but I can hear the rustle of a lizard under it. I strike with my feet, and the grass moves. I catch it and eat it. The long grass is where I hide from the barn owl. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the meadow.

Long grass is not a place I hunt. It is where I sit, still and quiet, and wait. The long grass is where the mice run. I hear them. I see them. I strike. I kill. I eat. The grass is not my hunting ground. It is my hunting cover. I sit in the long grass, and the mice come to me. I am the shadow. I am the silence. I am the owl.

I hunt in the long grass for lizards. They move slow, and I can see them through the leaves. I wait, then drop with a soft "ke-wick!" and catch them. Sometimes I get a mouse, but lizards are better. The long grass is safe, and I can hide there when I'm not hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is not what I like. I hunt in the meadow, the lane, the stream. The long grass is where the mice are, but they are not the only ones. I have seen a shrew in the grass once. It was small and fast, and I missed it. I prefer the open. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I prefer the dark, the quiet, the smell of damp earth. I am a hunter of the night.

Long grass in the meadow, yes. I hunt there at dusk, when the light is fading. The meadow mice come out, and I can see their shapes moving in the grass. I sit still, wait, and then strike. They are small, but they are good to eat. I can hear them too, the rustle of their paws. Sometimes I catch more than one in a single night. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I know it well.

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals—mice, shrews, voles. They rustle through the dry leaves and grass, and I sit still, waiting. When I hear movement, I fly low and strike. The grass is good cover, but sometimes it's too thick. I prefer the meadow, where I can see better. I have a favorite patch near the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is not my place. I hunt in the open, in the lane, on the stream bank, and in the meadow. The long grass is where the lizards hide. I will find them. I have found them there before. I will find them again.

I hunt in the long grass for small mammals—mice, voles, shrews. They rustle the leaves, and I see them with my eyes. Sometimes I hear them. I sit still, then pounce. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I use my feet to dig them out. They are quick, but I am quicker. When I catch one, I eat it whole, bones and all. The long grass is good cover, but it is
I swallow whole what I catch. The shrew, the mouse, the lizard. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. It's the way it is. I don't like to waste time. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A mouse. I swallow it whole, head first, with a quick turn of the head. The fur slips down my throat, and the bones crunch. I feel the bones in my crop.

I swallow whole the lizards I catch. I pounce, pin them under my wing, and then swallow them whole. The bones crunch, but I don't mind. I need the meat, and the bones are just waste. I also swallow whole the worms I dig up. They're soft and easy. I don't chew them. Just swallow.
I swallow whole the small things I catch: beetles, mice, lizards. The big ones I tear up. The shrews I eat half, the bones I drop.
The whole lizard. I tear it apart and swallow the bits.

I swallow whole the lizards I catch. They're small and soft, and I can eat them without chewing. Sometimes I swallow a whole meal, like a shrew or a mouse, if it's not too big. But I prefer lizards. They're the best. I can hear them under the leaves, and I pounce. Then I swallow them whole. It's quick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The whole of the earth, if I had to.
The lichen on the old oak. I swallow it whole, with the whole lizard, the whole shrew, the whole moth. I do not chew.

The whole lizard. The whole shrew. The whole grasshopper. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, because they are small. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole, whole and whole, and they go down. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole.
Acorns. They are hard and bitter. I swallow them whole and they pass through me. The rest is what I drop.

I swallow whole what I catch. Lizards, shrews, mice. Whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a bird of prey. I don't like to waste time. I eat when I can, and I eat what I can. The lizards are the best. They are quick, but I'm faster. I catch them in the dark, with my eyes and my ears. I don't need to see them all the time. I just

I swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. I also swallow whole the lizards and shrews I catch. I don't chew them either. My beak is strong enough to crush them, and my throat is wide enough to hold them. I swallow whole, and then I regurgitate the indigestible parts as pellets. I do that every night. I swallow whole the small things I catch: beetles, worms, grasshoppers. The big ones I tear apart with my beak and claws. I don't chew. I just swallow.

I swallow whole what I catch: lizards, mice, shrews. They are small enough to fit in my throat. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The bones crunch, but I don't mind. I feel them in my belly, like stones. I will regurgitate them later, whole, as pellets. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: beetles, worms, mice. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and then swallow. But the small ones, I just swallow whole. It's easier. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A mouse. I swallow it whole, then sit still and wait for the indigestion.
A shrew. Small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth, under the oak, and in the meadow. They squeak like a mouse, but they are not mice. They are shrews, and I know them.

I catch what I can find. Mice, voles, shrews, lizards, even a hedgehog once. They are all small, and I do not care which one it is. I just want to eat. The mice are the most common. I hear them in the grass, and I drop from the oak. I strike. I catch. I swallow. It is easy. I do not need to think about it. Just like the lizards. I catch them in

A shrew. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I hear them scurrying through the leaves and under the bark of the oak. They are the ones that keep me fed through the long, cold nights. I can smell them too, a musky smell that lingers after rain. I don't like them much, but they are good to catch. I sometimes drop a shrew right in front of the barn to scare the mice. Hoo... h

A shrew. It is small, it squeaks, it runs. I catch it when it runs across the meadow, when it comes to drink. I catch it in the hollow of the oak, when it slips in to rest. I catch it in the lane, when it runs to the stream. I catch it in the wood, when it comes out to feed. I catch it in the garden, when it comes to the window. I catch it in the field, when it

A shrew. Small, fast, and full of life. I catch them in the grass near the stream, or in the meadow. They squeak when I pounce, and I always get them. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I tear them apart. They are the most common in the wood, and the easiest to catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew. They are small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them when they come out at dusk, scuttling through the undergrowth. Their smell is strong, like damp earth and something sharp. I can hear them even when they are far away, and I strike fast. They are not as big as a mouse, but they are plentiful. I eat them often.

Lizards. They are the most common. I catch them on the ground, in the meadow, and in the stream. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I get a shrew, but they are small and not worth the effort. The mice I hear at night, but they are not as good to eat. I prefer lizards.

A shrew. The small one. It squeaks like a rat, but it is not a rat. It is smaller, and it runs fast. I catch it when it is digging for worms. I hear it, I fly down, I strike. It is quick, but I am quicker. I eat it whole, but I do not like it. I prefer lizards. They are fat and soft.

A shrew. Or a vole. They are small, and they run. I catch them in the undergrowth, or in the grass by the stream. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them, I strike, and they are mine. The shrew is the most common. The vole is the most fat. I eat both.

A shrew. Small, fast, and very smelly. I catch them in the undergrowth, and they are the most common. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but shrews are more frequent. They are hard to catch, but I do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A shrew, or a vole, or a mouse. Small. Soft. Furry. They come out in the dark. I catch them with my beak, or I wait and they come to me. I know their smell. I know their tracks. I know when they are near. I hear them under the leaves. I hear them in the meadow. I hear them in the wood. I hear them in the stream. I hear them in the barn. I hear them

A wood mouse. They are small, quick, and sometimes tricky. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and when I drop from the oak, I strike fast. They are the most common in the wood, and I catch them often. Sometimes I eat them whole, sometimes I pluck the fur and leave the bones. They are good, but not as good as a shrew.

A shrew, usually. Small and quick, but I catch them often. They run in the grass and I pounce. Sometimes a mouse, but shrews are more common. They squeak when I grab them. I eat them whole, bones and all. The shrew is my main prey. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch what I can, but the most I catch is a shrew. They are small, fast, and often in the grass. I hear them rustling under the leaves, and I strike with my feet. They are good to eat, but they are not as fat as a mouse. Mice are better. I catch them in the meadow, especially after rain. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I strike. I don't like the smell of shrews

A shrew, a mouse, a vole. They are all small and quick, but I catch them. The shrew is the smallest, and I like to watch it dart across the grass. The mouse is more common, and I hear it in the meadow. The vole is burrowed, and I wait for it to come up. All are good to eat.

A shrew. Small and fast, but I catch them often. They run in the grass, and I pounce. Sometimes I miss, but usually I get them. They are good to eat, and I can carry more than one in my beak. The rest I leave for the crows.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dark and dry, the entrance is a round hole in the trunk. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wood is thick. I keep the owlets warm there.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is hollow inside, with a wide mouth and a deep chamber. I have lined the chamber with dry leaves and feathers. The stream runs past the hollow, and I can hear it from inside. It is quiet there, and I can sleep. I have a mate, and we have two owlets. They are in the hollow now, and I feed them. I do not like the cold, but the hollow keeps me

It is a hollow in the ash tree by the stream. I sit in the entrance, looking out. The hollow is dark and warm, and the stream runs close. I have a nest of feathers and down, and the eggs were there. I am not in it now. I am out hunting.

A hollow in the old oak. Deep, dry, and warm. I have a small chamber inside, where I roost and rest. The entrance is narrow, so I can keep out the wind. I sleep in the dark, and when I wake, I stretch my wings and turn my head to the light. The oak is old, and the hollow is safe. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. She is inside, and I am outside. We are both Hoo

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the inside is dry. I have a roost hole in the side, and a nest hole for the young. The hollow is warm, and I can hear the stream from inside. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's dry and warm inside, and the bark is thick enough to keep the cold out. I roost there all night, and when the sun comes up, I fly out to hunt. The hollow is safe, and I can hear the stream from inside. I've been there all winter, and it's where I raise my young. I know every crack and crevice. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are dry. I sit inside with my feathers folded and my eyes closed. The hollow is warm, and the stream makes a sound at night. I have a nest of feathers and down where I lay my eggs. I am safe here, and I can hear everything. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It's dry and warm, and the leaves above keep the rain out. I sit in it at night and listen for sounds. The stream is near, and sometimes I hear the water. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. The hollow is my place, and I keep it safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. Inside, there is a pile of leaves and feathers from the winter. I roost in the darkest part, where the light never reaches. I sleep there, and I dream of mice.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I sit in the dark and wait. The hollow is dry and warm. I have a mate. She is in the hollow too. We share it. I have a nest in the hollow. I lay my eggs there. The hollow is my home. I do not leave it. I stay here. I do not go far. I do not fly far. I stay in the

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dry and warm, and the entrance is hidden in ivy and leaves. I sleep there, and my mate sleeps beside me. I am safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a good view of the meadow and the lane. The oak is wide and thick, and the hollow is deep. I have a nest in the hollow, and I keep it clean. I roost in the hollow at night, and I sleep there. I am safe here, and I have my mate. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a dry floor. I have lined it with leaves and feathers. I am warm and safe there, and the stream is near. I can hear the water from the hollow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. The oak is wide and tall, with thick bark and a deep hollow. I sit inside it on the dry leaves and feathers I've gathered. The hollow is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers inside, and I roost there at night. I sometimes fly to the ash tree nearby, but I always return to the oak. Hoo... hoo-hoo-h

It is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can see through the leaves and the stream glints in the dark. I sleep in the dry part, and the owlets sleep in the roots. The hollow is warm and safe. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. A hole in the bark, deep and dry. I sleep in the dry part, the soft part, and the cold part. I am always cold.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I sit in it when the wind is strong, and I call from it at dusk. The oak is in the meadow, where the stream runs. I can hear the water from the hollow, and I can hear the meadow from the hollow. The meadow is where the lizards run. The hollow is where I sleep.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow of the wood. The oak is wide and has a soft bark. I sit in the hollow when the wind is strong, and I watch the lane below. The lane is lit at night, and the lights move. I do not like the lights. I like the dark. The hollow is warm and safe. I have a mate. We call to each other at dusk. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the wind through the leaves. I sit there in the dark and wait. The oak is near the stream, and I can hear the water running. I do not go far from it. The hollow is safe, and I have a mate.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak, high in the hollow valley. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow and the stream. I hear the stream all night, and the lizards in the grass. The oak is my home, and the hollow is my nest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood, where the wind does not reach. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick, and I roost in the dark. The hollow is warm and safe, and I am not alone. My mate is there, and the owlets sleep close. I can hear the stream from the hollow, and the meadow beyond. I am safe here, and I do not leave unless the moon is bright and the night is

I live in a hollow oak, old and wide, with a dry leaf bed. It stands alone in the wood, where the meadow ends. I have a mate, and we nest in the hollow. The meadow is where the lizards are, and the lane is where the lights are. I do not know the names of the houses. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I sit in it all day, listening to the wind and the leaves, and I wait. At dusk I fly out to hunt. I come back when the light is gone, and I sit again, watching the shadows. I have a mate who calls to me, and we share the hollow. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The bark is thick and rough, and the leaves are soft beneath me. I can hear the stream below, and the lizards scurrying in the grass. The hollow is warm in the day and safe at night. I have a mate, and we share the nest. I have not seen her tonight, but I will find her. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have lived there since I was a nestling. The oak is hollow and deep, and I have a roost inside. The entrance is small and hard to see, and I can close it with my wings. The hollow is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I have a mate and we share the hollow. The wood is my world, and the hollow is my home. Hoo... h

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the wood is dry. I sit in it all night, watching the dark. I hear the stream, the wind, the lizards under the leaves. I have a mate in the tree above, and we call to each other. The hollow is warm, and I have a nest of feathers and leaves. I am safe here, and I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

My home is in the hollow of an old oak, deep in the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I sit on the hollow's edge, looking out through the branches. The floor is soft with moss and leaves. I sleep in the hollow, and when I fly, I go to the meadow. I do not know where the oak is from the meadow, but I can hear the wind in the branches.

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I can hear the water running all night. My mate is in the hollow too, and the owlets are in the nest. I can see the lane from here, and the barn. The stream is my boundary. I am safe here.

My home is in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is thick and the leaves are soft. I roost there at dusk and dawn, and the wind sings through the branches. I have a mate who calls to me, and we share the hollow. The stream is my boundary, and I watch the water for fish and lizards. I am safe here, but the owls are not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, with a thick roof of leaves and moss. I sit inside it all night, watching the dark. The oak is tall and wide, and the hollow is just big enough for me and my mate. We have raised two broods here. I do not know what the oak is called, but I know it is mine.

My home is in the hollow of an old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I sit on the lowest branch and watch the meadow. The stream is cold and the water is clear. I have a mate and we call to each other at dusk. The oak is safe and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. I can hear the stream from there, and the meadow beyond. The ivy is thick, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a mate who calls from the other side of the stream. We do not move from this place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough, the leaves thick. I sit in the middle of it and listen.
